facts.text: Despite its name, the white-breasted woodswallow is not a true swallow; it belongs to the Artamidae family alongside butcherbirds, currawongs and the Australian magpie.
facts.quote: The name "woodswallow" is a misnomer as they are not closely related to true swallows. Instead, they belong to the family Artamidae, which also includes butcherbirds, currawongs and the Australian magpie.

facts.text: The white-breasted woodswallow is the only woodswallow whose tail is completely black, with no white on it at all.
facts.quote: Their completely black tail makes them the only woodswallow lacking white on the tail.

facts.text: Males and females look identical, while juveniles wear browner, heavily striated plumage with a buff chest.
facts.quote: Males and females are identical in appearance. Juveniles have a more brownish plumage around their head and mantle that is usually heavily striated. They have a buff tint on their chest and a brownish bill with a dark tip.

facts.text: It is one of the few passerines that can soar, thanks to its large, pointed wings and agile flight.
facts.quote: The white-breasted woodswallow has large, pointed wings and is very agile in powered and gliding flight. It is fast-flying and is one of few passerines that can soar.

facts.text: Small but feisty, these birds are territorial and will gang up to mob larger birds in defence.
facts.quote: Even with their small statue, they can be aggressive birds whom are quite territorial with groups mobbing larger birds as a form of defense.

facts.text: Famous huddlers, they squeeze tightly together on branches or powerlines to stay warm and save energy.
facts.quote: They are social birds, well known for their habit of huddling up together tightly in flocks, usually along a branch or powerline. This behaviour enables the birds to maintain heat and conserve energy.

facts.text: A female invites copulation by spreading her wings in a V over her back, trembling, waggling her tail and quietly making an 'eep' call.
facts.quote: The female sexual display to invite copulation includes extending the wings over the back in a V, whilst trembling toward a male/s, then waggling the tail and quietly making an 'eep' call.

facts.text: They are cooperative breeders, and both sexes help build the nest, incubate the eggs and feed the young.
facts.quote: They are cooperative breeders, with birds other than parents assisting with care for offspring. Both sexes participate in building nests, incubating eggs and feeding young birds.

facts.text: Resourceful nesters, they will recycle abandoned magpie-lark nests as their own, and their clutches of 2 to 5 eggs hatch after 15 days of incubation.
facts.quote: Woodswallows are also known to recycle abandoned magpie-lark nests to use as their own. The normal clutch size is between 2 and 5 eggs. These are tapered oval-shaped and cream or pinkish in color with darker brown speckles. The eggs are incubated for 15 days.

facts.text: Though its brush-tipped tongue suggests a nectar feeder, it mainly eats insects caught in flight, occasionally sipping flower nectar.
facts.quote: Despite having a bifurcated (divided) brush-tipped tongue, which is usually associated with nectar feeders, woodswallows are insectivores primarily feeding on insects caught on the wings in flight or from a perch, and occasionally feeding on the nectar of flowers.
